questions.title: What exactly is being rescaled in LongRoPE: position index n or the RoPE frequencies, and are Eq. (1) and Eq. (2) consistent?
questions.question_body: In standard RoPE, the rotation angle in the i-th 2D plane is $n / \beta^i$ (with $\beta = \theta^{2/d}$). The paper's Eq. (1) writes the encoding as $[\cos(n\theta_0), \sin(n\theta_0), \ldots]$ with $\theta_i = \theta^{-2i/d}$, while Eq. (2) (the unified interpolation form) looks like $\cos\big(n / (\lambda\, \beta)^i\big)$, which I read as rescaling the denominator. Later, Eq. (3) uses an indicator $\mathbb{I}(\hat\lambda_i, \hat n)$ multiplying $n/\beta^i$. I'm confused about which quantity is conceptually being scaled: $n$, $\beta$, or the angle directly? Could the authors reconcile these notational variants and state the exact implementation (e.g., do you compute $\cos((n/\lambda_i)/\beta^i)$ for $n \ge \hat n$, or equivalently $\cos(n/(\lambda_i\beta)^i)$)?

questions.title: How does LongRoPE define interpolation vs. extrapolation when $\lambda_i \in [1, s\times1.25]$?
questions.question_body: The text says PI uses a uniform scale $\lambda = s$ (interpolation), and that NTK mixes interpolation and extrapolation, while YaRN extrapolates for high-frequency dimensions. In LongRoPE's search space, $\lambda_i$ ranges from 1.0 to $s\times1.25$, with 1.0 called "direct extrapolation". But if the angle becomes $(n/\lambda_i)/\beta^i$, then $\lambda_i > 1$ reduces the angle (seems like interpolation), and $\lambda_i < 1$ would increase the angle (seems like extrapolation). Why is $\lambda_i = 1.0$ labeled extrapolation? Is there a sign or reciprocal convention I am missing (e.g., is $\hat\lambda_i = 1/\lambda_i$ the true scaling on the angle)?

questions.title: What guarantees symmetry between queries and keys under LongRoPE’s non-uniform scaling per dimension?
questions.question_body: RoPE rotates both queries and keys so that their dot products encode relative positions. If LongRoPE applies per-dimension rescale factors $\lambda_i$ and a position threshold $\hat n$, is the exact same transformation applied to both queries and keys for the same head? Are there any corner cases where Q and K could end up misaligned (e.g., due to caching, chunking, or dynamic switching of $\hat n$) that would break the relative position property?

questions.title: How is the monotonic constraint $\lambda_i \le \lambda_{i+1}$ theoretically justified beyond NTK intuition?
questions.question_body: The search imposes $\lambda_i \le \lambda_{i+1}$ so that higher-frequency (lower $i$) dimensions get less interpolation and lower-frequency (higher $i$) dimensions get more. This is motivated by NTK and Fourier intuition. Is there a more formal argument that monotonicity in $\lambda_i$ is near-optimal, or could non-monotone patterns yield better fits for some models? Did you empirically test removing this constraint at smaller $d$ to quantify potential gains versus search cost?

questions.title: Why does keeping the first $\hat n$ tokens unscaled improve performance, and how should $\hat n$ scale with target length $L'$?
questions.question_body: Finding 2 claims that preserving the first $\hat n$ tokens without interpolation helps because early tokens often receive high attention. However, the optimal $\hat n$ depends on the target length ($8$k vs. $16$k had different optima). Is there a heuristic or theoretical scaling law for $\hat n$ as a function of extension ratio $s = L'/L$ or of model depth/width? Also, do you apply a hard switch at $n = \hat n$ or a smooth schedule (e.g., a taper) across the first few hundred tokens to avoid discontinuities?

questions.title: How does per-dimension scaling interact with head-wise RoPE usage in multi-head attention?
questions.question_body: RoPE is typically applied per head, and different heads may emphasize different frequency bands. LongRoPE searches one set of $\{\lambda_i\}$ per RoPE dimension index $i$. Is this shared across all heads, or do you allow head-specific scaling? If shared, could performance benefit from per-head $\lambda_{h,i}$, and did you attempt a reduced-parameter variant (e.g., a few groups across heads) to balance search cost and head specialization?

questions.title: Why does non-uniform scaling preserve short-context performance better than PI/NTK/YaRN, and why is a separate short-length search still needed?
questions.question_body: The paper says non-uniform scaling preserves "key dimensions and token positions" to reduce information loss, which helps both as initialization and for 8x non-finetuned extension. Yet after achieving 2048k, you still run a separate short-length search (e.g., 4k/8k) to recover performance. Can you explain mechanistically why the first search (optimized for 256k or beyond) cannot maintain short-length quality, and what properties distinguish the second search results (smaller max $\lambda$) that specifically benefit short contexts?

questions.title: What prevents overfitting the search to the few PG19/Books3 samples used for perplexity evaluation?
questions.question_body: During search, you compute perplexity on 5 PG19 validation samples (within 256k) or 3 Books3 samples (over 512k). Given the huge search space, how do you avoid overfitting to these specific books? Did you measure generalization by evaluating candidate $\{\lambda_i, \hat n\}$ on a held-out set never used during the search, or by cross-validation across documents? Any signs of instability when switching to different corpora or domains (e.g., code vs. literature)?

questions.title: How does the progressive extension avoid catastrophic drift when re-searching on a fine-tuned 256k model?
questions.question_body: The method fine-tunes to 256k and then runs a second search to reach 2048k without further training. Why does this not undo the benefits of the 256k fine-tuning? Intuitively, the weights adapted to a certain geometry of RoPE angles at 256k. After you change the angle scaling again for 2048k, what keeps the representations coherent? Is there evidence that the 256k-adapted weights land in a basin that is robust to subsequent frequency adjustments?

questions.title: Can you quantify the "attention dispersion" claim that motivates short-context recovery?
questions.question_body: The introduction argues that at extremely long lengths, attention becomes "dispersed" and performance at short contexts degrades. Could you provide a quantitative measure of dispersion (e.g., entropy of attention distributions, head sparsity metrics, or effective context length usage) comparing baseline RoPE vs. LongRoPE at 4k and 256k? It would help connect the geometric crowding of positions with observable changes in attention behavior.

questions.title: How is computational feasibility maintained when evaluating perplexity at lengths up to 256k during search?
questions.question_body: The search evaluates many candidates and computes perplexity at target length $L'$ (up to 256k for the first stage). What engineering tricks make this feasible? For example: chunked evaluation with sliding windows, KV cache reuse across candidates, FP8/INT8 matmuls, sub-sequence sampling, or early stopping of bad candidates? A rough wall-clock and GPU-hour estimate for a typical 128k and 256k search would clarify practicality.

questions.title: How does LongRoPE compare to dynamic NTK scaling that depends on current sequence length at inference?
questions.question_body: Dynamic NTK adjusts scaling as a function of the actual sequence length. LongRoPE instead searches fixed $\{\lambda_i\}$ (plus $\hat n$) per target window and then even switches to different searched sets for 4k/8k at inference. Conceptually, is LongRoPE approximating a piecewise-constant dynamic schedule across lengths? Would a hybrid that learns a continuous function $\lambda_i(\ell)$ of current length $\ell$ outperform the discrete switching strategy?

questions.title: What is the relationship between per-dimension $\lambda_i$ and an effective change of RoPE base $\theta$?
questions.question_body: Standard RoPE uses $\theta_i = \theta^{-2i/d}$, equivalently angles $n/\beta^i$ with $\beta=\theta^{2/d}$. If LongRoPE applies different $\lambda_i$ per dimension, is this equivalent to using a different base $\theta_i'$ per $i$ (i.e., changing $\beta$ per dimension)? If so, could this be interpreted as learning a non-geometric frequency ladder instead of a single-base geometric progression, and does that viewpoint suggest constraints or regularization that might improve search stability?

questions.title: Does the hard threshold at $\hat n$ introduce artifacts around that boundary, and did you try a smooth schedule?
questions.question_body: Eq. (3) applies $\mathbb{I}(\hat\lambda_i, \hat n)$ such that angles for $n < \hat n$ are unscaled and for $n \ge \hat n$ are scaled by $1/\lambda_i$. That creates a discontinuity at $n = \hat n$. Did you observe any boundary artifacts (e.g., spikes in loss) near that position? If so, did you try a smooth transition (e.g., a cosine ramp for $n \in [\hat n - w, \hat n + w]$) and how did it compare?

questions.title: How does LongRoPE interact with KV caching and streaming/infinite attention methods?
questions.question_body: Since LongRoPE changes the angle schedule, how should one handle KV cache entries created under one set of $\{\lambda_i, \hat n\}$ and later reused when the active set switches (e.g., switching to short-context factors for a short query after processing a long context)? Is it necessary to flush caches when switching factor sets, or can you safely mix caches as long as the same factors were used for the tokens within that cache?

questions.title: Why is 8x non-finetuned extension stable while 16x is not, and what breaks first beyond 8x?
questions.question_body: You report stable 8x extension without fine-tuning, but existing methods spike beyond 2x. What specifically degrades beyond 8x for LongRoPE: layer-wise attention alignment, head specialization, value drift, or numerical issues in angle periodicity (e.g., too many wraps)? Any diagnostic plots (e.g., per-head perplexity vs. length) that reveal the first failure mode?

questions.title: How comparable are the baseline training setups, and could data differences confound the results?
questions.question_body: For Mistral you follow YaRN with 16k training length and Long-Data Collections, while for LLaMA2 you use RedPajama chunks at 128k/256k. Since data and training lengths differ across models and baselines (Together-32k, Code LLaMA, LongLoRA, etc.), how do we ensure a fair apples-to-apples comparison? Did you also run LongRoPE on the exact settings used by the strongest baselines to isolate the impact of positional scaling alone?
